questions.q: What is the difference between data and information?
options: Data and information are the same thing
Data is raw facts; information is data that is processed and has meaning
Information is raw facts; data is the meaning
Data is only numbers; information is only text
questions.hint: Which one is 'raw' and which one 'tells you something'?
questions.explain_simple: Data = raw facts, like 20, 22, 25. Information = those facts organized so they mean something.
questions.explain: Data is raw, unprocessed facts. When we organize or process data so it has meaning, it becomes information.

questions.q: Which one is INFORMATION (not just data)?
options: The average temperature this week was 24°C
questions.hint: Look for the sentence that tells you something useful.
questions.explain_simple: A list of numbers is only data. A sentence like 'the average was 24°C' gives meaning, so it is information.
questions.explain: Lists of numbers or names are raw data. 'The average temperature this week was 24°C' is processed data with meaning — information.

options: A computer learns patterns from data, instead of a person writing every rule
A robot that works in a factory
A program that only stores data in a table
A faster type of internet connection
questions.hint: Think: who writes the rules — a person, or the computer from data?
questions.explain_simple: In ML, we give the computer many examples. It finds the pattern itself.
questions.explain: Machine Learning means a computer learns patterns from data and uses them to make predictions, without a person writing every rule by hand.

options: A library for drawing charts only
A Python library for working with tables of data (rows and columns)
questions.hint: Think of Excel, but inside Python.
questions.explain_simple: Pandas works with tables: read a file, clean it, filter rows, count, group.
questions.explain: Pandas is a Python library for loading, cleaning and analyzing table data (rows and columns).

questions.q: In Pandas, what is the name of the main table object?
questions.hint: Its name has the word 'Frame' in it.
questions.explain_simple: A DataFrame is a table in Pandas. It has rows and columns, like an Excel sheet.
questions.explain: The DataFrame is Pandas' main object: a table with rows and named columns.

options: Fast math with numbers and arrays
questions.explain_simple: NumPy = Numerical Python. It does math on many numbers very fast.
questions.explain: NumPy (Numerical Python) gives fast arrays and math functions. Pandas and many ML libraries are built on it.

options: A library for training neural networks
A library for reading CSV files
A Python library for making charts and graphs
questions.explain_simple: Matplotlib draws charts: line charts, bar charts, histograms, and more.
questions.explain: Matplotlib is the basic Python library for plotting — line, bar, scatter, histogram charts.

options: A library for fast math with arrays
A table library that replaces Pandas
A chart library built on Matplotlib, for nicer statistical charts with less code
A tool for writing Python code
questions.hint: It is also for charts, and it uses Matplotlib inside.
questions.explain_simple: Seaborn makes beautiful charts (like heatmaps) with short code. It uses Matplotlib under the hood.
questions.explain: Seaborn is built on Matplotlib. It makes statistical charts (heatmap, boxplot, pairplot) look good with less code.

questions.q: You want to open a CSV file as a table. Which library do you use?
questions.explain_simple: pd.read_csv('file.csv') opens the file as a DataFrame (a table).
questions.explain: Pandas reads CSV files into a DataFrame with pd.read_csv(). The other libraries are for math or charts.

questions.q: What is the standard way to import Pandas?
questions.hint: The short name is the first letters of 'pandas'.
questions.explain_simple: Everyone writes: import pandas as pd. Also: numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns.
questions.explain: The common short names are: pandas → pd, numpy → np, matplotlib.pyplot → plt, seaborn → sns.

options: A number with a decimal point, like 2.5
A whole number with no decimal point, like 7 or -3
questions.explain: An integer (int) is a whole number without a decimal point: 7, 0, -3, 2026.

questions.hint: A float has a decimal point and NO quotes.
questions.explain_simple: float = number with a dot: 3.14, 0.5, 9.99. If it has quotes, it is text.
questions.explain: 3.14 is a float (a number with a decimal point). "3.14" in quotes is a string, 10 is an int, True is a boolean.

options: A number with a decimal point
questions.explain_simple: str = text. We write it inside quotes: "hello", 'Ali'.
questions.explain: A string (str) is text. In Python we put it inside quotes: "Tashkent" or 'hello'.

questions.q: What is the type of "100" (with quotes)?
questions.explain_simple: "100" has quotes, so Python sees it as text (str), not a number.
questions.explain: Anything inside quotes is a string. "100" is str; 100 without quotes is int.

questions.q: age = 25, price = 9.99, name = "Ali". Which one is which?
options: age = float, price = int, name = str
age = str, price = float, name = int
age = int, price = float, name = str
age = int, price = str, name = float
questions.hint: Whole number → int. Decimal point → float. Quotes → str.
questions.explain_simple: 25 is a whole number (int). 9.99 has a dot (float). "Ali" has quotes (str).
questions.explain: 25 → int (whole number), 9.99 → float (decimal point), "Ali" → str (text in quotes).
